introduction: This guide opens with a distinction: the Prophets knew that Christ would be martyred, and their knowing did not cause it. The readings that follow are of several kinds: warnings meant to be heeded, about race in America and about the arsenal of Europe; dates drawn from Daniel; hopes for Iran, for the twentieth century, for women, for a common language and for flight; and many promises, to a community under pressure, that “ere long” the hidden will be plain. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá also says that prophecies are not what the proof rests on. Beside the readings stand the scriptures they draw on and some unexpected witnesses: Milton on foreknowledge, Jefferson and Lincoln on slavery’s reckoning, Tennyson’s airy navies, Morse’s first telegram. Jeremiah’s rule that a warning may avert what it announces runs through the whole. The doubters are Bacon and Hume on why predictions seem to come true, the Talmud on calculating the end, Ezekiel’s proverb that every vision fails, and Hardy and Arnold, who looked at the same years and saw less light.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that foreknowledge is “not the cause” of what is foreknown, and that what is written “will definitely come to pass, but we servants must strive”. How do Milton, Rabbi Akiva and Blake each hold certainty and effort together?

Several readings warn so that the thing warned of may not happen. By Jeremiah’s rule and Jonah’s experience, what would count as the success of such a prophecy, and how should the warnings about race and about war in this guide be read in that light?
“There are many prophecies but we do not use them as proofs.” Why not, given how many this guide gathers? Consider Bacon’s remark and Jesus’ refusal of a sign.

Some of these hopes have dates on them: the twentieth century as a century of peace, East and West embracing, a common language. Set Hardy, Orwell and Kipling beside them. How should a reader today receive a hope whose century has passed?

Many readings promise that “ere long” what is hidden will be manifest. What does Ezekiel’s proverb about failing visions demand of such promises, and what did Jeremiah’s letter to the exiles ask of people who wanted a quick end?

The faithful are told that their deeds will one day be proclaimed and that those who reproached them will boast of knowing them. How does the Sermon on the Mount’s warning about being seen bear on taking comfort in that?

outside.why: “Did their knowledge and awareness cause the martyrdom of Christ? No.” Milton has God make the same distinction about the fall of man: foreknowledge had no influence on their fault.

Knowing beforehand, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, is “not the cause” of what is known. Rabbi Akiva’s sentence holds the two together without explaining them: everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is granted.
“Thinkest thou that He would have commanded thee to pray for that which would never come?” These are the words of the prayer meant.

What the Supreme Pen has written “will definitely come to pass, but we servants must strive and surge and cry out”. Blake holds a promise in the same way, as work: I will not cease from mental fight till we have built Jerusalem.

If the union of white and black “is not realized, erelong great difficulties will arise … and may end in bloodshed”. Jefferson, a slaveholder, had written the same fear into his book on Virginia: I tremble for my country when I reflect that God is just.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá warns of enmity ending in bloodshed. Lincoln, at the end of a war that had come, read it as a judgment: every drop of blood drawn with the lash paid by another drawn with the sword.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá is reported as foretelling “the destruction of America”, and elsewhere in this guide as hoping the dynamite will not explode. Jeremiah states the rule under which such words are spoken: if that nation turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do. Is a warning that works a failed prediction?
“Arise with high resolve … that this world-consuming fire may not blaze forth.” Jonah’s forty days were announced without conditions, and the city believed, fasted and was spared.

The Holy Books give “the glad tidings of a certain Day” when “the banner of the Most Great Peace” would be hoisted. Micah’s is the best known of those tidings: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation.
This is the passage ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes “in reference to the Promised One that must come after Christ”.
“This is a well-guarded secret … That it will be revealed is predestined.” Daniel asks what the end will be and is told: the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end.

Whoever claims a Revelation before a thousand years “is assuredly a lying impostor”, and whoever reads the verse otherwise has gone astray. Paul protects his message with the same double lock: though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel.
This is the verse asked about. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads its days as solar years and its blessing as a time when “the believers will rejoice”.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives the 1,335 days a date. The Talmud forbids the exercise for a practical reason: when the date passes, people say he will never come. What keeps the reading’s reckoning from that outcome?
“There are many prophecies but we do not use them as proofs.” Jesus offers the same alternative: believe me for the very works’ sake.
“Is there need for any one to say the sun is shining? Its own appearance is sufficient.” Jesus refuses a sign from heaven to people who already have what they need to judge.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sets prophecies aside as proofs and points to what Bahá’u’lláh did in chains. Bacon gives a reason for the same caution: men mark when predictions hit and never when they miss. Why, then, does this guide collect so many? What are they for?
“The newly born babe of that Day excels the wisest and most venerable men of this time.” Jesus says it of John the Baptist: he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

The Holy Spirit causes words “to stream from the tongue of poets, the significance of which they themselves are oftentimes unable to apprehend”. Socrates had noticed it when he questioned the poets of Athens: like diviners, they say many fine things and do not understand them.

The Báb says of a verse of Ḥáfiẓ that its mystery is “now concealed”. Shelley claims the same for all poets: mirrors of the shadows which futurity casts upon the present; the words which express what they understand not.

“The Day of Judgment hath come, and mankind hath stood before the LORD.” The Apocalypse describes a day that no one could fail to notice. What must the Day of Judgment mean for the reading’s sentence to be true of a world that did not notice?
“Open your eyes that you may behold the lights.” Isaiah: arise, shine; for thy light is come.
“I send you the glad tidings”, five times over. Isaiah on the one who brings such news: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings.
“Erelong … the fast asleep will be awakened.” Paul: now it is high time to awake out of sleep; the night is far spent, the day is at hand.

“The day will soon come when the light of Divine unity will have so permeated the East and the West that no man dare any longer ignore it.” Habakkuk: the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
“When the appointed hour is come, there shall suddenly appear that which shall cause the limbs of mankind to quake.” Jesus: in such an hour as ye think not.
“Hesitate not, though it be for less than a moment, in the service of His Cause.” The Preacher’s counsel under uncertainty: in the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand.
“Whatever is recorded in these Epistles has happened.” Deuteronomy’s test of a prophet is whether the thing follows and comes to pass.

Some prophecies “came to pass after two years; others … after five, ten and twenty”. Hume would ask whether it is more remarkable that a forecast was inspired or that, in twenty years, thrones should fall. What in the record answers him?
“Following a universal convulsion, the sun of justice will rise.” Malachi sets the same sunrise after a day that burns as an oven.
“All this was foretold by the Prophets of old.” Amos: the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
Bahá’u’lláh quotes this verse for “the severity of these days”. In Isaiah it goes on: the lofty looks of man shall be humbled.

“The inflammable materials stored in the infernal arsenals of Europe.” Forty years and two wars later a general who had become president counted what arsenals cost: every gun that is made is a theft from those who hunger.
“I said plainly that the continent of Europe had become like unto an arsenal.” Jesus on those who read the sky and cannot discern the signs of the times.
“A smoldering volcano … lieth hid beneath the soil of Europe.” Yeats wrote after it had burst: things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.
“The Movement of the Left will acquire great importance. Its influence will spread.” The movement’s own founding call, of 1848: working men of all countries, unite!
“If the people of the world do not turn … great danger lies ahead.” Moses puts the future to Israel in the same conditional: I have set before you life and death; therefore choose life.
“Undoubtedly the standard of universal peace shall be unfurled.” Tennyson’s couplet gave the nineteenth century its phrase for it: the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
“If the letters which … Bahá’u’lláh sent to the rulers of the world had been put into action, this war would not have occurred.” Caesar on the man who warned him: he is a dreamer; let us leave him.

Among the things foretold is “Universal Peace which shall be eventually established”. Kant drew up terms for a perpetual peace and still doubted the material: nothing quite straight can be made of it. On what does the reading’s “shall” rest?

Future kings of Iran, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes, will cause “the renown … of past monarchs to be wholly forgotten”. Shelley’s sonnet is about how thoroughly kings are forgotten. What kind of greatness does the reading mean, that would not end the same way?
“Iran will become the most prosperous of all lands.” Isaiah’s picture of a land restored: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
“Erelong shall that dust-heap become a rose-garden … Its ancient glory will be restored.” Isaiah: they shall build the old wastes, the desolations of many generations.
“I cherish the hope that it may become the envy of the world.” Tagore hoped for his own country in the same years, and measured the hope by what its people would be: where the mind is without fear.

“Erelong shalt thou witness East and West embracing each other as two lovers.” Kipling’s line says never the twain shall meet; his next lines say that two strong men, met face to face, undo it. Which half of his ballad has the century borne out?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá bids the twentieth century be “the century of lights … of international peace”. Hardy stood at its first evening and could see no cause for the thrush’s joy, only “some blessed Hope, whereof he knew and I was unaware”. How does the reading’s wish read now, and was it a prediction?
“Human equality will be universally established.” In 1948 the nations wrote it down as their starting point: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

The reading expects a “new social form” in which equality is established. Orwell’s fable records what one movement for equality became within a generation: some animals are more equal than others. What would keep a new social form from that end?
“The right to vote is the inalienable right of women.” The Seneca Falls convention had said so in 1848, in Jefferson’s cadence: all men and women are created equal.

“The entrance of women into all human departments is an irrefutable and incontrovertible question.” For centuries the question was closed by a verse: let your women keep silence in the churches. How does a prediction like the reading’s stand toward a text like that?
“The love and effort put into Esperanto will not be lost.” Zamenhof’s own hope for it was modest and exact: that each person would know two languages, his own and one in common.
The Báb asked for means of swift communication; “in a short time the telegraph appeared”. The first message sent on Morse’s line in 1844 was these four words from the book of Numbers.
News carried at the speed of lightning was, in Job, one of the things only God could do: canst thou send lightnings, that they may go and say unto thee, Here we are?

“Everything will be renewed, in every department. This generation cannot be compared to the past.” The Preacher: is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? Which things did the century renew, and which did it leave as he found them?
“People will travel at ease from one city to another” by air. Isaiah, seeing ships come home, asks who these are that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their windows.
Arms will be carried and used “from the air”. Tennyson had seen both halves seventy years earlier: the heavens filled with commerce, and a ghastly dew raining from the nations’ airy navies.

America “will lead all nations spiritually”. The oldest American form of the thought came with a warning attached: we shall be as a city upon a hill, and if we deal falsely we shall be made a story and a by-word.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises the cities and prosperity of America and its promising future. Du Bois, nine years before, had named what stood in the way: the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line. How do the two sayings, and the warning in the first part of this guide, fit together?
“The West will have replaced the East, radiating the light of Divine Guidance.” The Gospel’s figure for the coming runs the same way across the sky, from the east even unto the west.
“Rejoice, O Holy Land.” Isaiah’s words to that land: the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it, the excellency of Carmel and Sharon.
“This plain will be built and will become inhabited by a happy people.” Amos: they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards.

“Be not sad owing to the present ruin of the House. The time of its building shall come.” Haggai to those who wept remembering the first temple: the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former.
“We must destroy and build it again.” Jesus says it of a temple and is misunderstood; he spoke, John adds, of the temple of his body.
The first House of Worship is “the mother”, and “a hundred thousand” shall be born of it. The kingdom is like the least of seeds, which becomes a tree.
The House of Worship “will become the center” from which teaching spreads to all parts of the world. Isaiah: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.

A “divine edifice” is to be completed, and great effects are expected from it. Solomon, dedicating his, asked whether God will indeed dwell on the earth, when the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him. What do the readings expect a building to do?

“Although the importance of this divine Institute is not very evident now, yet in the future it will be clear and plain as the sun.” Paul says of his own small beginnings at Corinth that he planted and another watered, and God gave the increase.
“Ye shall surely behold a Pillar of Fire extending upward to the Supreme Apex.” The image is from the Exodus, where it goes before the people by night to give them light.
“The radiance of that Light is now concealed from view … yet ere long that world-illumining light will shine forth.” Jesus: a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
The Caucasus may become a place where “the gazelles of unity amble and stroll in its fields and mountains”. Isaiah: the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb.
“Ere long these grievous days and severe times shall pass away.” The psalm: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
“Look not at the present moment only, like those who lack insight.” Paul: we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.
“This is a promise that shall not prove false.” Habakkuk is told as much of his vision: at the end it shall speak, and not lie; though it tarry, wait for it.

“Ere long … Ere long.” Ezekiel’s contemporaries had a proverb about prophets who talked like that: the days are prolonged, and every vision faileth. How long is “ere long”, and who is entitled to say that a promise has failed?

“These numbered days shall pass away, and We shall behold the sincere ones in pavilions of glory.” Paul: the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed.
“This Branch will grow after it is cut off from this world below … and it shall bear such fruits.” Jesus, of his own death: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá is asked about the time “after my departure” and promises that the Spirit will run in the body of the world. Jesus to his disciples: it is expedient for you that I go away.

In prison Bahá’u’lláh “always said … that this captivity would not last very long”. Jeremiah wrote the opposite to the exiles in Babylon, against prophets who promised a quick return: build houses, and seek the peace of the city. When is the hopeful word the true one?

“God shall, through it, soon conquer the hearts of all who dwell on earth.” Arnold, in the same years, heard faith’s long withdrawing roar. A century and a half later, which of the two forecasts reads more like the world, and does the answer settle anything?

The tradition gives the Qá’im a sign from Joseph: “imprisonment and dissimulation”. Joseph’s own reading of his imprisonment, said to the brothers who caused it: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
“Soon the results and fruits of steadfastness and firmness will become manifest”, and the violators will be in loss. In the parable the sorting waits: let both grow together until the harvest.
“Soon will the dense clouds disperse … and the brilliant morn will shine forth.” Shelley’s last line asks it as a question that expects yes: if Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
“We hope that this autumn of pain and tribulation will pass and the life-giving spring will come.” The Song of Solomon: lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.

“Through the blood which they shed the earth hath been impregnated … Ere-long shall she tell out her tidings.” In Genesis the earth already speaks of the first blood shed on it: the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.
The blood of the martyrs, says the prayer, has made the earth fruitful. Tertullian’s phrase for it has lasted eighteen centuries: the blood of Christians is seed.
“On that day thou shalt behold the waverers, men and women alike, frustrated of their hopes.” Paine on the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot, in the worst month of a war that was later won.
Souls are promised who “would give sight to the blind, and would make the deaf to hear”. The phrases are Isaiah’s: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened.
Bahá’u’lláh promised ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that such souls would be raised up. Jesus makes a like promise about those who come after him: greater works than these shall he do.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes Christ on the thief who comes when the owner is unaware. Paul draws the practical point from the same saying: let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch.
“Every one of you, even as a shining star, will radiate in the firmament of your country.” Daniel: they that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever.
“Ere long shall the saplings that have been planted bring forth wondrous and sublime fruits.” The psalm: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

“Today the station of deeds and their fruit is hidden from sight”, and it will be “proclaimed from the pulpits”. Jesus: that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.

The reading consoles the faithful with the promise that their deeds will become known. The Sermon on the Mount warns against doing them in order to be seen. How can one be glad of the promise without wanting the notice?
All shall be transformed: “tyranny into justice … poverty into wealth, and want into abundance.” Isaiah: every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low.
The reading lists seven reversals decreed “as an irrevocable fate”. Mary’s song sings three of them as already done: the mighty put down, the hungry filled, the rich sent empty away.
“Erelong shalt thou see a great transformation occurring in thy family.” The Gospel notes of Jesus’ own family, before any such change: neither did his brethren believe in him.
A husband “still distant and heedless” will one day feel honoured by his wife’s faith. The usual rule, which the promise overturns: no prophet is accepted in his own country.
The words ‘Abdu’l-Bahá puts in the mouths of former critics are those of Joseph’s brothers in the Qur’an, when they stand before the brother they sold.
The heedless “will … utter words of praise for the friends” and envy their servitude. The psalm: the stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
“Such a state of bliss as will be the envy of the queens of the world throughout the ages.” A village girl says it of herself in Luke: from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

jeremiah-if-that-nation-turn.text: At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them

john-for-the-very-works-sake.text: Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works' sake

john-greater-works.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father

matthew-least-in-the-kingdom.text: Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he

isaiah-full-of-the-knowledge.text: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea

isaiah-enter-into-the-rock.text: Enter into the rock, and hide thee in the dust, for fear of the Lord, and for the glory of his majesty. The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day

numbers-what-hath-god-wrought.text: Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel: according to this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought

job-send-lightnings.text: Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go and say unto thee, Here we are

isaiah-fly-as-a-cloud.text: Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their windows

isaiah-earth-is-my-footstool.text: Thus saith the Lord, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest

isaiah-build-the-old-wastes.text: And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations

haggai-latter-house.text: The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the Lord of hosts

john-destroy-this-temple.text: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Then said the Jews, Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days? But he spake of the temple of his body

psalm-joy-in-the-morning.text: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning

romans-not-worthy-to-be-compared.text: For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us

john-expedient-that-i-go.text: Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you

genesis-blood-crieth.text: And the Lord said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper? And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground

luke-nothing-covered.text: For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known. Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops

isaiah-every-valley.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it

isaiah-beauty-for-ashes.text: To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified

matthew-last-shall-be-first.text: So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen

psalm-stone-builders-refused.text: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner. This is the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes

luke-call-me-blessed.text: My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed

habakkuk-knowledge-of-the-glory.text: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea

quran-preferred-thee-above-us.text: They said: By Allah, verily Allah hath preferred thee above us, and we were indeed sinful.

milton-foreknowledge-no-influence.text: they themselves decreed / Their own revolt, not I; if I foreknew, / Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault, / Which had no less proved certain unforeknown
milton-foreknowledge-no-influence.author: John Milton

plato-poets-like-diviners.text: not by wisdom do poets write poetry, but by a sort of genius and inspiration; they are like diviners or soothsayers who also say many fine things, but do not understand the meaning of them
plato-poets-like-diviners.author: Plato

lincoln-drawn-with-the-lash.text: Fondly do we hope, fervently do we pray, that this mighty scourge of war may speedily pass away. Yet, if God wills that it continue until all the wealth piled by the bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of unrequited toil shall be sunk, and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash shall be paid by another drawn with the sword, as was said three thousand years ago, so still it must be said "the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether
lincoln-drawn-with-the-lash.author: Abraham Lincoln

rights.note: Address of a President of the United States.

shelley-hierophants.text: Poets are the hierophants of an unapprehended inspiration; the mirrors of the gigantic shadows which futurity casts upon the present; the words which express what they understand not
shelley-hierophants.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

hardy-darkling-thrush.text: So little cause for carolings / Of such ecstatic sound / Was written on terrestrial things / Afar or nigh around. / That I could think there trembled through / His happy good-night air / Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew / And I was unaware
hardy-darkling-thrush.author: Thomas Hardy

jefferson-tremble-for-my-country.text: Indeed I tremble for my country when I reflect that God is just; that his justice cannot sleep forever
jefferson-tremble-for-my-country.author: Thomas Jefferson
jefferson-tremble-for-my-country.work: Notes on the State of Virginia
